major.name: Political Science - BA - Public Policy

items.label: Public Policy
items.notes: POLI 117 and POLI 117R cannot both be taken for credit toward the major.

narrative: All courses taken for a political science major must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C- or better must be earned.
Lower-division courses POLI 27, POLI 28, POLI 40, POLI 197I, and POLI 197SD may not be used to satisfy requirements in the political science major or minor.
Students may not receive credit for both POLI 5 and POLI 5D; for both POLI 10 and POLI 10D; for both 11 and 11D; 12 and 12D; 13 and 13D; 30 and 30D.

Two upper-division courses in a field may be substituted for that field's lower-division course. However, these courses cannot also be used to satisfy the upper-division course requirements for a concentration of that field.
At least ten courses in political science must be taken in residence at UC San Diego. A total maximum of six courses may be taken elsewhere and applied toward the major.
Students must maintain an overall 2.0 GPA in the major.
Courses taken to satisfy requirements for the major may not be taken Pass/Not Pass with the exception of a maximum of two independent study courses (POLI 199).

Students who pass the Advanced Placement (AP) Tests in American or Comparative Politics may petition to be exempted from taking POLI 10 or 10D or 11 or 11D (respectively) ... students must pass with a score of 5.
Law and Society 101, Contemporary Legal Issues, may be used in fulfilling the twelve upper-division course requirement for the political science major.

nodes.title: Data Analytics for the Social Sciences
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with POLI 5D.) Students engage in hands-on learning with applied social science problems. The course teaches the basics of data management and collection, data analysis, and data visualization. To perform these analyses, students learn how to code in various programming software, including Excel, Stata, and R. Students may receive credit for only one of the following courses: ECON 5, POLI 5, POLI 5D, ECON 5R.

nodes.title: Data Analytics for the Social Sciences
nodes.description: Introduction to probability and analysis for understanding data in the social world. Students engage in hands-on learning with applied social science problems. Basics of probability, visual display of data, data collection and management, hypothesis testing, and computation. Students may receive credit for only one of the following courses: ECON 5, ECON 5R, POLI 5, POLI 5R, POLI 5D, or POLI 5DR.

nodes.title: Introduction to Political Science: American Politics
nodes.description: This course surveys the processes and institutions of American politics. Among the topics discussed are individual political attitudes and values, political participation, voting, parties, interest groups, Congress, presidency, Supreme Court, the federal bureaucracy, and domestic and foreign policy making. POLI 10 is Lecture only, and POLI 10D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 10 and 10D.

nodes.title: The Presidency
nodes.description: The role of the presidency in American politics. Topics will include nomination and election politics, relations with Congress, party leadership, presidential control of the bureaucracy, international political role, and presidential psychology.

nodes.title: The U.S. Congress
nodes.description: This course will examine the nomination and election of congressmen, constituent relationships, the development of the institution, formal and informal structures, leadership, comparisons of House with Senate, lobbying, and relationship with the executive branch.

nodes.title: American Political Parties
nodes.description: This course examines the development of the two major parties from 1789 to the present. Considers the nature of party coalitions, the role of leaders, activists, organizers, and voters, and the performance of parties in government.

nodes.title: Interest Group Politics
nodes.description: The theory and practice of interest group politics in the United States. Theories of pluralism and collective action, the behavior and influence of lobbies, the role of political action committees, and other important aspects of group action in politics are examined.

nodes.title: Social Networks
nodes.description: This class explores the many ways in which face-to-face social networks have a powerful effect on a wide range of human behaviors. With a foundation in understanding real-world networks, we can then consider how these networks function online.

nodes.title: How to Win or Lose an Election
nodes.description: This course explores the various aspects of a political campaign including campaign organization, vote targeting, political parties, social media, fundraising, polling, media interactions, and more. These areas are examined citing specific examples from federal, state, and local campaigns.

nodes.title: Race and Ethnicity in American Politics
nodes.description: This course examines the processes by which racial and ethnic groups have/have not been incorporated into the American political system. The course focuses on the political experiences of European immigrant groups, blacks, Latinos, and Asians.

nodes.title: Race in American Political Development
nodes.description: Readings examine how the multiracial character of the United States has shaped the broad outlines of American politics. Cases include the founding/the Constitution, southern politics, social organization in formerly Mexican regions, the New Deal, consequences of limited suffrage.

nodes.title: Political Psychology
nodes.description: We begin with hypotheses about how people develop political attitudes, and methods to test those hypotheses. The second half focuses on emerging cognitive neuroscience insights, including brain imaging, and asks how these inform theories of political cognition, affect, and behavior.

nodes.title: Politics in Washington
nodes.description: Examines Washington as a political community, its institutions, culture, and history. In addition to its elected officeholders and senior government officials, it examines Washington’s subcommunities: the national news industry, diplomatic service, the representation of interests.

nodes.title: Perspectives on Race
nodes.description: This course looks at race in American politics from a variety of perspectives. We may consider psychological, genetic, neuroscience, economic, political, sociological, and legal views of what drives powerful dynamics of race in our country.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Racial Politics
nodes.description: This course explores how race shapes outcomes in American democracy through in-depth exploration of key issues in American politics. Topics include race in the voting booth, immigration, discrimination, and inter-minority conflict.

nodes.title: Organized Interests
nodes.description: This course provides a theoretical and practical examination of political parties, interest groups, and social movements in the United States.

nodes.title: Politics, Policy, and Educational Inequality
nodes.description: Education is often thought of as “the great equalizer” but in the US and around the world, many governments fail to ensure that all citizens have access to high-quality educational opportunities. Why? This course will give students the conceptual tools to understand who shapes education policy decisions, through what channels, and how those policy decisions affect the quality and equity of education. Emphasis is on the US, but analyzed in comparative perspective.

nodes.title: Data Analysis and United States Politics
nodes.description: This course examines U.S. politics from a computational point of view. Through in-class work and hands-on assignments, we will use data analysis tools to collect, analyze, and visualize data related to various facets of federal level politics in the US. Students will develop statistical and computational skills that will assist them in advanced analyses of elections, legislative outcomes, lobbying, and other dynamics of the lawmaking process in Congress.

nodes.title: Asian American Politics in the United States
nodes.description: This class is a survey of historical and contemporary issues in Asian American politics in the US; race and ethnicity in the context of U.S. politics; comparisons of racial and ethnic group experiences in the US with those experienced by racial and ethnic groups elsewhere; Asian American access to the political system through political participation.

nodes.title: Gender and American Politics
nodes.description: This course examines the role of gender in American politics. First, we consider how gender plays a role in political opinions and behavior among citizens. Then, we turn to the elite level and examine whether women legislate differently than their male counterparts and how the broader political context influences patterns of women’s representation. We conclude by sorting through explanations for why women are underrepresented in political office and assess implications for American democracy.

nodes.title: The Politics of Race, Ethnicity, and Immigration
nodes.description: This course examines the interplay between racial/ethnic identity and politics. How do race and ethnicity become politicized? What role does ethnic or racial identity play in political behavior and decision-making processes? To what extent do political institutions and institutional design reinforce the salience of ethnic or racial identity in politics? We will be taking a comparative approach to this topic, and cover readings in both American politics and comparative politics literature.

nodes.title: American Political Development
nodes.description: Examines selected issues and moments in the political history of the United States, comparing competing explanations and analyses of U.S. politics. Likely topics include the founding, “American exceptionalism,” change in the party system, race in U.S. politics, the “new institutionalism.”

nodes.title: Urban Politics
nodes.description: (Same as USP107) This survey course focuses upon the following six topics: the evolution of urban politics since the mid-nineteenth century; the urban fiscal crisis; federal/urban relationships; the “new” ethnic politics; urban power structure and leadership; and selected contemporary policy issues such as downtown redevelopment, poverty, and race.

nodes.title: The Politics of Regulation
nodes.description: Politics and policy-making issues in regulation. Themes: regulation versus legislation; general versus specific grants of regulatory power; market versus command mechanisms; private property; and risk assessment. Emphasis on American regulatory policy, examples from current regulatory debates (e.g., health care and environment).

nodes.title: California Government and Politics
nodes.description: This survey course explores six topics: 1) the state’s political history; 2) campaigning, the mass media, and elections; 3) actors and institutions in the making of state policy; 4) local government; 5) contemporary policy issues; e.g., Proposition 13, school desegregation, crime, housing and land use, transportation, water; 6) California’s role in national politics.

nodes.title: Politics and Policymaking in Los Angeles
nodes.description: (Same as USP 113) This course examines politics and policymaking in the five-county Los Angeles region. It explores the historical development of the city, suburbs, and region; politics, power, and governance; and major policy challenges facing the city and metropolitan area.

nodes.title: Politics and Policymaking in San Diego
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: (Same as USP 115) This course examines how major policy decisions are made in San Diego. It analyzes the region’s power structure (including the roles of nongovernmental organizations and the media), governance systems and reform efforts, and the politics of major infrastructure projects.

nodes.title: Bending the Curve: Solutions to Climate Change
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with SIO 109 or SIO 109R.) Climate change is an urgent global problem affecting the lives of hundreds of millions of people, now and for the foreseeable future. This course will empower students to confront climate change as critical actors to innovate creative cross-disciplinary solutions that integrate technology, policy and governance, finance, land use, and social/educational dimensions. Students may not receive credit for POLI 117 or 117R and SIO 109 or SIO 190R.

nodes.title: Bending the Curve: Solutions to Climate Change
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with SIO 109 or SIO 109R.) Climate change is an urgent global problem affecting the lives of hundreds of millions of people, now and for the foreseeable future. nodes.title: Politics of Human Rights
nodes.description: What do we mean by “international human rights”? Are they universal? This course examines human rights abuse and redress over time, and across different regions of the world. From this empirically grounded perspective, we critically evaluate contemporary human rights debates.

nodes.title: United States Foreign Policy
nodes.description: United States foreign policy from the colonial period to the present era. Systematic analysis of competing explanations for U.S. policies—strategic interests, economic requirements, or the vicissitudes of domestic politics. Interaction between the US, foreign states (particularly allies), and transnational actors are examined.

nodes.title: National Security Strategy
nodes.description: A survey of American strategies for national defense. Topics may include deterrence, coercive diplomacy, limited war, and unconventional warfare.

nodes.title: Politics of Immigration
nodes.description: Comparative analysis of attempts by the United States and other industrialized countries to initiate, regulate and reduce immigration from Third World countries. Social and economic factors shaping outcomes of immigration policies, public opinion toward immigrants, anti-immigration movements, and immigration policy reform options in industrialized countries.

nodes.title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
nodes.description: (Same as USP 101) This course will explore the process by which the preferences of individuals are converted into public policy. Also included will be an examination of the complexity of policy problems, methods for designing better policies, and a review of tools used by analysts and policy makers.

nodes.title: Introduction to Policy Analysis
nodes.description: In this course, students will use their knowledge of the political and economic foundations of public policy making to conduct research in a wide variety of public policy problems.

nodes.title: Environmental Policy
nodes.description: This course will explore contemporary environmental issues such as global warming, endangered species, and land use. Students will be asked to analyze various policy options and to write case analyses. Policies may be debated in class.

nodes.title: Analyzing Politics
nodes.description: Politics are understood as the combination of individual preferences and decisions into collective choices. What are the issues involved in aggregating individual preferences, what is the choice of rules—formal and informal—for doing so.

nodes.title: The Politics of Public Policy
nodes.description: How do politics determine policy? In this course, students will be introduced to the skill of conducting a cost-benefit analysis, and then will discuss how political ideas, interests, and institutions often move policy outcomes away from those based on cost-benefit analysis.

nodes.title: Special Topic: Policy Analysis
nodes.description: An undergraduate course designed to cover various aspects of policy analysis. May be repeated for credit two times, provided each course is a separate topic, for a maximum of twelve units.

nodes.title: Policy Assessment
nodes.description: The use of real data to assess policy alternatives. Introduction to benefit/cost analysis, decision theory, and the valuation of public goods. Applications to health, environmental, and regulatory economic policy making.

nodes.title: Algorithms, Public Policy, and Ethics
nodes.description: The deployment of predictive algorithms for public policy optimization has increased in recent years across a variety of domains. This course will introduce key concepts, considerations, and concerns relating to algorithmic decision-making in policy processes. This includes understanding how data are used to make predictions, how predictions can be used to aid decision-making, the conditions under which these practices will be effective, and the important ethical dimensions of these practices.

nodes.title: Applied Data Analysis for Political Science
nodes.prereq_text: POLI 30 or POLI 30D or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course is an advanced introductory course for undergraduates. It will acquaint students with statistical methodology as it is used in the social sciences. It is assumed that the student has the mathematical background to progress through the materials a bit faster than in a true introductory course.

nodes.title: Making Policy with Data
nodes.prereq_text: POLI 5 or 5D or ECON 5 and POLI 30 or 30D.
nodes.description: This class explores how we can make policy recommendations using data. We attempt to establish causal relationships between policy intervention and outcomes based on statistical evidence. Hands-on examples will be provided throughout the course.

nodes.title: Advanced Social Data Analytics
nodes.prereq_text: POLI 5 or 5D or ECON 5 and POLI 30 or 30D.
nodes.description: An accelerated course in computer programming and data analytics for collecting, analyzing, and understanding data in the social world. Students engage in hands-on learning with applied social science problems, developing statistical and computational skills for sophisticated data manipulation, analysis, visualization.

nodes.title: Data Analysis for Policy Advice
nodes.description: This course is aimed at students interested in using their analytical skills to provide insights to decision-makers primarily in the government and nonprofit sectors. We will study the types of decision-makers that exist, what kinds of questions they typically have, the methods and data that are available to answer them, and how to go about packaging and delivering policy advice. These skills are taught using applied examples from public policy and administrative datasets.

nodes.title: Special Topics in Political Science Methodology
nodes.description: Special topics course in quantitative methods for political science and broader social sciences. May be taken for credit up to three times.
